This remarkably low hatchling mass necessitates an intense period of parental provisioning, as the tiny nestling possesses minimal energy reserves. The female, who bears the sole responsibility for nest construction and incubation, must balance the energetic cost of egg production with the demands of thermoregulating the clutch. The diminutive size of the hatchling means that even a brief interruption in brooding can be fatal, highlighting the critical importance of the female's consistent attendance until the chick is capable of limited thermoregulation. The successful transition from hatchling to a feather-growing nestling therefore depends heavily on this initial mass and the thermal regime provided by the attentive parent.

Females of this species attain an ultimate wet body mass of 3.1 grams [Wwi = 3.1 grams], a figure that represents the upper limit of adult somatic growth. This adult mass, coupled with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, dictates the species' high resting metabolic rate and its reliance on torpor during periods of cold stress or food scarcity. The interval between fledging and puberty is thus a critical period of behavioral and physiological refinement, during which the immature bird hones its foraging skills and learns to navigate the complex three-dimensional environment of the forest understory.
